Sir Charles Lloyd Jones (1878 to 1958) was an Australian businessman and patron of the arts, serving as Chairman of David Jones from 1920 until his death in 1958. A trained painter himself, he studied at the Julian Ashton Art School in Sydney and then the Slade School of Fine Art in London. He went on to shape Sydney's art scene: he was a co-founder of the magazine Art in Australia in 1916, and he established the David Jones Art Gallery in the Elizabeth Street store in 1944. He was also a committed supporter of William Dobell, and the gallery's first exhibition was devoted to him. He was knighted in the 1951 New Year's Honours. His collection was later offered as The Lloyd Jones' Collection, James R. Lawson, Sydney, 9 April 1981.

Charles Lloyd Jones 爵士（1878-1958）為澳洲商人及藝術贊助人，自1920年起出任 David Jones 百貨公司主席，直至1958年辭世。他本身亦習畫，曾先後就讀於悉尼 Julian Ashton 藝術學校及倫敦斯萊德美術學院。他對悉尼藝術界影響深遠：1916年與人共同創辦《Art in Australia》雜誌，1944年於伊莉莎白街分店設立 David Jones 藝廊。他長期支持畫家 William Dobell，藝廊首展即為 Dobell 個展。1951年新年授勳時獲封爵士。其收藏其後由悉尼 James R. The Xi (觿) toggle originally evolved from an animal tooth used for untying knots, its chief feature being a pointed tip at one end. In earliest times people made them from animal bone or tooth, worn on the body for undoing knots. Once made in jade, the xi gradually lost its original function and became a symbolic pendant ornament. For a similar piece, see Palace Museum, Beijing, acc.no.新00128735.

觽最早由解結之獸牙演變而來。《說文解字》曰：「觿，佩角，銳端可以解結。」其主要特徵是一端呈尖角。最早古人以獸骨或獸牙製作，佩帶於身用於解結。以玉製觿後，逐漸喪失了其原始功能，成為象徵性佩飾件。《說苑修文篇》曰：「能治煩決亂者佩觿。」可知觿在古人眼裡有治煩決亂之意。（摘自故宮博物院網站）比較一相似白玉觿，見北京故宮博物院acc.no.新00128735。

Huang Musong was a military commander and politician of the late Qing and early Republic Period. After the 13th Dalai Lama died in Dec 1933, Huang was appointed Special Envoy to offer sacrifices to the late Dalai Lama in Jan 1934 (the 23rd year of the Republic). In Aug 1934 he travelled to the Potala Palace to perform the memorial rites, and he conferred on the 13th Dalai Lama the posthumous title 'Hu Guo Hong Fa Pu Ci Yuan Jue Da Shi' (Great Master of Universal Compassion and Perfect Enlightenment, Protector of the Nation and Propagator of the Dharma). In Mar 1935 he was appointed Chairman of the Mongolian and Tibetan Affairs Commission. The accompanying scanned photograph is inscribed by Huang: 'A photograph taken on the journey into Tibet as envoy, dressed in lama's robes. For Mr Zaizhi to keep, respectfully presented by Huang Musong. The 24th year of the Republic [1935].'

比較上海寶山明墓出土、現藏上海博物館之相類牌飾，惟無款識，詳見此處。與本拍品相同，其雕工「間隙処作毛地」，該館官網指出此種做法頗為罕見。

黃慕松，清末民初軍事將領、政治家。1933年12月，十三世達賴喇嘛圓寂。1934年（民國23年）1月，黃慕松被任命為致祭達賴專使。1934年8月赴西藏拉薩布達拉宮致祭，並追封十三世達賴喇嘛「護國弘法普慈圓覺大師」。1935年3月，被任命為蒙藏委員會委員長。留影中黃自署：⌈奉使入藏在途中著喇嘛服裝之撮影。載之先生惠存，黃慕松敬贈。民國廿四年。⌋

款識：唯守璞，任自然。保太和，以永年。同治己巳（1869），石壽山人作。

Shishou Shanren was the studio name of Wang Heng 汪鑅 (1817 to 1882), a native of Ningxiang in Hunan province (now part of Changsha). A scholar, painter and calligrapher, he was particularly renowned for engraving stone tablets and carving seals. His seal carvings were compiled as Shishou shanren yincun, and he is listed in Zhongguo meishujia renming cidian, p. 462. His signed snuff bottles are found in a variety of materials, including amber, hornbill, rock crystal and jade. Examples include one in the J & J Collection, illustrated by Moss, Graham, Tsang, The Art of the Chinese Snuff Bottle, no. 292, and sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 25 April 2004, lot 878; another sold at Christie's New York, 22 March 2007, Important Chinese Snuff Bottles from the J & J Collection, Part IV, lot 16, dated to 1839 (though utilising an earlier bottle); and one sold at Bonhams New York, 23 March 2026, lot 262.

Hugh Moss compiles a few such bottles and also includes a note on Wang in his essay The World in a Bottle in the World, accessed here.

石壽山人，乃汪鑅（1817-1882）齋號。汪，湖南寧鄉（今屬長沙）人，字嘯霞，號石壽山人，齋名石壽山房，為學者、畫家及書法家，尤以刻碑及篆刻著稱。其篆刻作品被輯為《石壽山人印存》，又見錄於《中國美術家人名辭典》，頁462。其署款鼻烟壺傳世者，取材多元，有琥珀、鶴頂紅、晶、玉等，包括J & J Collection藏一例，見Moss、Graham、Tsang著《The Art of the Chinese Snuff Bottle》，編號292，後於2004年4月25日香港佳士得拍賣，拍品編號878；另一例於2007年3月22日紐約佳士得「Important Chinese Snuff Bottles from the J & J Collection, Part IV」拍賣，拍品編號16，紀年相當於1839年（惟所用壺坯年代較早），以及邦瀚斯，紐約，2026年3月23日，拍品262。

Moss曾輯錄數件此類鼻煙壺，並於其文章〈The World in a Bottle in the World〉中對汪鑅有所論述，詳見此處。

Compare with a similar bottle, with near identical 'plum blossom' decoration, and also trace of red Guyuexuan mark, see Christie's, 23 Mar 2012, lot 1589. In the Crane collection, there are two bottles similar to the current lot, one with a bit more elaborate painting, however the same shoulder decoration and most likely identical mark, accessed here, the other, with almost the same painted decoration, no shoulder decoration nor mark, accessed here. Judging from the mark on the Crane bottle, it is understandable why the current lot, as well as the one sold at Christie's, only has faint traces of the mark left.

About the marked bottle, Balbach discusses that 18th-century bottles with Guyue Xuan marks, associated with the lakeside Jian Yuan (Garden of Reflection), tend to carry naturalistic enamelled subjects, unlike the formal, archaistic and religious Court style of Beijing. Prof. Peter Lam proposes that glass made in the Yuanming Yuan workshop was handed to the Ruyi Guan painters, also based in the Yuanming Yuan, for decoration; the Archives confirm the finer work was done there rather than at the Canchikou glass factory. If so, the early Guyue Xuan group came from the Imperial Household Workshops and should share the features of bottles with genuine Qianlong reign marks.

傳承：
香港榮豐，1972年1月31日，編號1360（V. Bruce鼻煙壺札記，編號56，及賬單）

Qianlong period monochromatic landscapes on copper bottles are more often in puce than in blue. The Ming-style landscapes in blue with reign mark are most famously done on snuff dishes, including the one from the Tuyet Nguyet and Stephen Markbreiter collection, sold at Sotheby's, Hong Kong, 4 Jun 2021, lot 1033, another at Christie's, Hong Kong, 12 Oct 2021, lot 11, and a third one published in 張榮，你應該知道的200件鼻烟壺，北京故宮博物院, Taipei, 2008, p.144.

Blue landscapes on bottles are rare, most of them probably not marked. See one in the Royal Ontario Museum, dated to the mid 18th to mid 19th century acc.no.925X64.8, and another from the Crane collection, accessed here. In the footnotes of the 'Crane' bottle, the comparison was drawn from copper enamel in other forms (such as a kettle), and porcelain bottles in underglaze blue from the Qing Dynasty - further evidence of the scarcity of such bottles.

Qianlong marks within a square border are rare on enamelled copper snuff bottles. The mark closest to that on the present bottle, on an example also dated to the Qianlong period, is illustrated in An Addicted Dedication: Chinese Snuff Bottles Christopher Sin's Collection, Hong Kong, 2013, p.380, pl.359. Another bottle dated to the Qianlong period is in the Palace Museum, Beijing, see 張榮，你應該知道的200件鼻烟壺，北京故宮博物院, Taipei, 2008, p.102, though the mark is of seal script and in black enamel.

傳承：

This bottle is, for the most part, a double layer, three-colour overlay. The inner pink layer forms the petals and parts of the leaves and rocks, while the outer layer of black and green accentuates the flower centres, the stems and the highlights on the leaves and rocks.

Unlike single layer multicolour overlay, in which the colours are applied as separate blobs using tubes or sticks, multilayer overlay is built up by dipping the base bottle in successive layers of colour. A five colour single layer bottle is relatively common, whereas a true five layer bottle is only rumoured to exist. In both cases the outer layers are carved and ground away to leave the design in relief against the inner colour, but dipping successive layers of different colours demands far greater control and forethought, and the results can sometimes be unpredictable. The colour of an outer layer may inevitably intrude into the design of an inner one, as seen in the present lot, where black appears at the tips of some of the daisy petals; whether by design or by chance, there is no way of knowing.

Curiously, three layers are visible at the base, where the green rocks are further highlighted in black, and the foot rim clearly reveals the pink, green and black in successive layers.

Black glass is often seen highlighting petals and leaves in this kind of multi-layer glass, for another bottle decorated similarly with pink flowers and black highlights, see The Au Hang Collection of Chinese Snuff Bottles, p.205, pl.141.

此瓶大體為雙層三色套料。內層粉紅料用以表現花瓣及部分葉片與山石，外層黑、綠二色則勾勒花蕊、枝莖，並點綴葉片與山石。

單層多色套料乃以料棒或料管將各色料分別點施於瓶身；多層套料則不同，係將胎瓶反覆蘸入不同顏色之料，逐層疊套而成。五色單層套料瓶較為常見，而真正的五層套料瓶則僅見於傳聞。兩者雖同樣須將外層料雕琢磨去，使紋飾以浮雕形式凸顯於內層底色之上，然逐層蘸套不同色料，所需之掌控與事先構思遠為精密，成品效果亦難盡在預料之中。外層色料難免滲入內層紋飾，如本品雛菊部分花瓣尖端即可見黑色，究屬有意為之抑或偶然所致，已無從考證。

饒有趣味的是，瓶底可見三層料色，綠色山石之上復以黑色點染；圈足亦清晰可見粉、綠、黑三色層層相疊。

此類多層套料鼻煙壺中，常以黑色料點綴花瓣及葉片，另一件同樣飾粉色花卉並以黑料點綴之例，見《區氏集壺精舍藏中國鼻烟壺》，頁205，圖版141。

Among snuff bottles there is a category known as the 'table bottle', referring to a larger vessel that is not readily carried on the person (that is, not of pocket size) and was instead intended to stand on a desk or table, either for appreciation or to hold a larger quantity of snuff.

Gold-inlaid jade snuff bottles are mostly flattened in form, though their shapes vary widely. The National Palace Museum, Taipei, holds several examples: a gourd-shaped bottle (acc. no.Guyu 005832N000000000, close in size to the present bottle, both nearly 8.0cm high), a tall bottle-shaped example (acc. no.Guyu 001657N000000000), and a squat bottle-shaped example (acc. no.Guyu 005630N000000000). There was also one from the Mary and George Bloch Collection, of tall and straight-sided shape, sold at Sotheby's, Hong Kong, 23 Nov 2014, lot 51. Among bottles of this type, an example carved from spinach-green jade, as with the present bottle, was sold at Bonhams, New York, 16 Mar 2015, lot 1097. The 'figure' carving in the front in the current lot is however extremely rare.

Private Collection, Hong Kong | é¦æ¸¯ç§äººçèA PAIR OF MIDNIGHT-BLUE-GROUND EMBROIDERED PRESIDENT'S ROUNDELS WITH TWELVE SYMBOLS OF SOVEREIGNTY
Circa 1914
embroidered on a midnight blue satin with two confronted dragons in looped and couched metal threads, their outlines further accentuated with coral beads, flanking the fu symbol at the centre, above them the Sun in coral beads, the Moon, three stars in fluffed and couched wavy threads, and the flames, again in coral beads, at the sides the pair of ritual cups and the axe, below, the water weed, the grain, the pheasant and the mountains, all within a border of clouds of blue, purple, and beige, various symbols and motifs done in fine and neat Peking knots, approx. 21.6cm wide each (2).

約一九一四年 民國三年大總統祭服十二章繡團成對

General Yuan Shikai (1859 to 1916) became President of the newly established Republic of China, and he harboured ambitions to become Emperor. In an act that truly embodied that ambition, he planned and performed a sacrifice to Heaven on 23 December 1914. In Imperial China, the sacrifice to Heaven was the single most important act of kingship, for to perform it was in effect a public statement that one held the Mandate of Heaven.

From 1912 the new Republic had a code of formal dress modelled on Western morning and evening wear. When Yuan Shikai revived the state sacrifices in 1914, the Political Council resolved that worship required a dress of its own. The Minister of the Interior, Zhu Qiqian, convened a committee whose memorial argued that clothes for receiving people and clothes for serving the spirits should not be the same. It pointed to Japan, whose Shinto priests still wore robes derived from the Tang, as proof that a modern state could keep a separate ritual dress. The committee chose the juebian (爵弁) cap of antiquity and the classical pairing of a dark upper garment and reddish skirt (玄衣纁裳), to be worn by all ranks from the head of state downwards. Yuan approved the proposal on 5 July 1914 and ordered it printed.

Thus were born The Regulations for Sacrificial Caps and Robes (《祭祀冠服制》), not unlike the Illustrated Standards of Ritual Objects of the Imperial Dynasty (《皇朝禮器圖式》) issued by the Qianlong Emperor. The Regulations divided sacrificial dress into five grades, and above these stood an attire to be worn by one person only: the President of the Republic. Its robe bore twelve roundels, each containing all twelve symbols of sovereignty, which in imperial China only the Emperor had the right to bear in full.

In earlier practice, the twelve symbols were divided between the upper and lower garments in a fixed sequence. The 1914 commentary notes that this order had already been changed since the Zhou, and proposes instead to gather all the symbols into one roundel (合其章為團), grading rank by the number of roundels. The solution kept the full imperial vocabulary for the head of state, while presenting it as a measured, classical hierarchy rather than a personal monopoly. The present roundels show the scheme exactly. Compare the current lot with a photocopy of the page from The Regulations.

Yuan's sacrifice at the Temple of Heaven, held at the winter solstice, was the first since the fall of the Qing. Within a year he had declared himself Emperor, and after his death in June 1916 the state sacrifices lapsed. The presidential robe was therefore officially in use for barely two years.

Few objects capture so precisely the uneasy moment between empire and republic. The Regulations reserved this attire for one man alone, and it was worn for less than two years before the demise of Yuan. Very little of the ritual dress made for Yuan's sacrifice is known to survive, which makes the present pair rare physical witnesses to the ceremony at the Temple of Heaven. In them, the twelve symbols of imperial sovereignty reappear on the dress of a republican President, a vivid record of the ambition that would lead, within a year, to the Hongxian throne.

More rank badges of the same era, unlike the twelve-symbol roundels, are known naturally. A nine-symbol badge of the first rank officials is illustrated in Making the Grade - The Badge of Rank III, Linda Wrigglesworth, London, 1996, p.18, and another one of seven-symbol, see Bonhams, Sydney, 2 Apr 2025, lot 6.

袁世凱（1859年至1916年）出任新成立之中華民國大總統，並懷有稱帝之志。民國三年十二月二十三日（1914年12月23日），他籌劃並親行祀天大典，此舉正是其野心的具體體現。在帝制時代，祀天為帝王最重要的禮儀；能行此禮者，實即昭告天下其承受天命。

民國元年起，共和國頒行禮服制度，取法西式大禮服與常禮服。民國三年，袁世凱恢復國家祭祀，政治會議議決祭祀應另定專用之服。內務總長朱啓鈐召集議訂，其呈文指出，接人之服與事神之服不宜混同；並舉日本神官神職之服多採唐制為例，說明現代國家亦可另設祭服。議訂者採用古制爵弁為祭冠，並以玄衣纁裳為祭服，自元首以至士庶通用。此案於民國三年七月五日奉批核准，並交付刊印。

《祭祀冠服制》由此誕生，其性質與乾隆皇帝所頒之《皇朝禮器圖式》不無相似之處。《祭祀冠服制》將祭服分為五等，而凌駕其上者，乃僅供一人穿著之服，即中華民國大總統之祭服。其衣繡十二團，每團皆具十二章；帝制時代，唯皇帝得兼用十二章。

古制十二章分繡於衣裳，各有定序。民國三年之說明書指出，周時已變更其序，故改為「合其章為團」，並以團數之多寡區分等級。此法既為元首保留完整的帝王章紋，又將之呈現為有度、合乎古禮的等級秩序，而非一人獨享之專權。

此對繡團正可印證其制。深藍緞地上，以盤金繡成雙龍相對，並以珊瑚珠勾勒，拱衛居中之黻紋。上方為珊瑚珠綴成之日，以及月、三星及火；兩側為宗彝及黼；下方為藻、粉米、華蟲及山，四周環以雲紋。請將本拍品與《祭祀冠服制》相關頁面之影印本比對。

民國三年冬至，即1914年12月23日，袁世凱於天壇祀天，為清亡以來首次。不及一年，袁氏即稱帝；民國五年六月袁氏逝世，國家祭祀隨之中輟，大總統祭服實際使用因而不過兩年。每件上衣本有十二團，此對當出自其中一件。

鮮有器物能如此精準地呈現帝制與共和交替之際的微妙時刻。《祭祀冠服制》規定此服僅大總統一人得用，而使用不過兩年，國家祭祀即告中輟。袁世凱祀天所製之祭服，存世者寥寥，此對繡團因而成為天壇祀天大典罕見的實物見證。帝王十二章重現於共和國大總統之祭服，生動記錄了不及一年後終致洪憲稱帝的政治野心。

同時期的其他官階補子傳世較多，自然較為人知。一品官員所用九章紋補子一例，著錄於 Linda Wrigglesworth，Making the Grade - The Badge of Rank III，倫敦，1996年，頁18；另一七章紋例子，見邦瀚斯悉尼2025年4月2日拍賣，第6號拍品。
